one_liner: Rust io_uring thread-per-core proxy framework (ByteDance, archived) edging nginx on small-body HTTPS proxying; slower on plain HTTP.
what_it_does: Monolake is a Rust framework (monolake-core, monolake-services) for building L7 proxies and gateways on ByteDance's monoio runtime, plus a reference proxy binary driven by a TOML file that defines listeners (TCP or Unix socket), routes to upstream URIs, optional TLS certificate and key, and the runtime type and worker count; replacing the file hot-reloads it for new connections. It proxies HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 downstream (HTTP/1.1 upstream by default) and Thrift TTHeader, with services composed through its own service-async Service trait rather than Tower. It is not an nginx replacement: different config format, and nginx-compatible rewrites, upstream health checks and gRPC were still open feature issues when the repository was archived.
how_it_is_fast: Thread-per-core: each worker thread runs its own monoio runtime on io_uring (the default runtime type, 32768 ring entries, falling back to the epoll 'legacy' driver if io_uring is unavailable) with no work stealing, so a connection's state stays on one core. The HTTP and Thrift codecs (monoio-http, monoio-thrift) are written for io_uring's owned-buffer I/O, upstream connections are pooled (ConnectionReuseHandler), and monoio is built with its splice feature. HTTPS terminates in rustls 0.21 through monoio-rustls built with unsafe_io, which saves one buffer copy per operation; the project itself never explains its HTTPS edge.
when_to_use: Building a custom Rust gateway on Linux that must speak Thrift/TTHeader or convert HTTP to Thrift, where you are prepared to own the code.
TLS-terminating reverse proxy for small responses (512 B to 4 KiB) on Linux with io_uring, where the published charts show about 1.1-1.2x nginx requests per second.
Studying a production-used (at ByteDance) monoio service-composition design (service-async, certain-map, hot-reloaded service factories) before building your own.
when_not_to_use: Plain HTTP proxying: nginx was equal or faster in every published run (Nov 2024 4-vCPU run: 161,101 vs 187,973 req/s tiny, 0.86x; medium 0.79x; README charts nginx ahead or tied).
Large HTTPS responses (16-64 KiB), where the README charts put nginx ahead.
Anything needing security updates or support: archived 2025-08-29 with a 'no longer recommended for use' notice, pinned to Rust nightly and rustls 0.21.
Hostname upstreams: upstream DNS lookups were not cached (issue #114, open at archival; 105 req/s and 23,514 wrk2 timeouts until upstreams were given as IPs).
Teams wanting nginx feature parity (rewrites, LB health checks, gRPC were open issues #152, #158, #150).

integration.form: crate (monolake 0.3.0, monolake-core, monolake-services 0.3.2 on crates.io, last published 2024-11-16) plus a reference proxy binary
integration.dependencies: monoio 0.2, monoio-http, monoio-transports, monoio-thrift, service-async, certain-map, hyper 1 with monoio-compat; default tls feature pulls rustls 0.21 (monoio-rustls) and native-tls (monoio-native-tls, OpenSSL on Linux)
integration.min_toolchain: Rust nightly (rust-toolchain.toml); monolake-services at HEAD uses edition 2024
integration.platforms: Linux with io_uring (docs say kernel 5.1+) for the fast path; epoll fallback on Linux, kqueue on macOS; only x86-64 (AMD EPYC) measured
integration.thread_safety: Thread-per-core: each worker thread runs its own monoio runtime and gets its own service instances from the broadcast config; library-level guarantees not documented

gotchas: The HTTPS comparison is rustls versus OpenSSL: the per-server TLS `stack` setting defaults to rustls (TlsStack #[default] Rustls at both the Nov 2024 benchmark commit d02397f and HEAD) and the benchmark's monolake.toml sets no stack, while nginx came from the Amazon Linux package; the catalogue's earlier note that the default is native-tls is wrong (the default cargo feature only compiles native-tls in alongside rustls).

Harness flaw in the only tabulated run (benchmark/ at d02397f, removed before archival): wrk2 offered different -R target rates per proxy (HTTPS tiny 160,000 for Monolake vs 150,000 for nginx; HTTP tiny 200,000 vs 210,000; HTTP large 100,000 vs 10,000, where Monolake logged 618 timeouts vs nginx's 22), nginx's HTTPS locations used proxy_buffering off while its HTTP ones buffered, and the large rows move about 10-12 Gbit/s for every proxy, so they look link-bound (derived from page data). The current README charts have no scripts, configs or tables in the repo.

monolake-services enables monoio-transports' rustls-unsafe-io, which turns on monoio-rustls unsafe_io; that crate's Cargo.toml warns the I/O future must not be dropped before it returns ready. Monolake applies keepalive and upstream read timeouts, so audit cancellation paths before trusting it with untrusted clients.
Upstream hostnames are resolved without caching (issue #114); `cargo run --config` fails with 'expected string but found table in list' unless written `cargo run -- --config` (issue #162).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Monolake only when you want a Rust proxy framework with Thrift support on io_uring and accept an archived codebase; for a plain reverse proxy that beats nginx on HTTP too, routez (1.26x on keep-alive upstream proxying) is the stronger catalogued claim, and statico has a monoio variant for fixed in-memory responses.
verified_claims_summary: On an AWS c6a.8xlarge (AMD EPYC 7R13, Amazon Linux 2023, kernel 6.1) the README charts (images only, nginx 1.24.0 with unstated build and config, load generator not named) show Monolake at about 1.15-1.19x nginx's HTTPS requests per second for 512 B-4 KiB bodies and 1.07-1.18x at 8-16 worker threads, a tie at 8 KiB, and nginx ahead for 16-64 KiB HTTPS and for plain HTTP. The only tabulated run (Nov 2024, wrk2, 4-vCPU c5a.xlarge proxy in front of an nginx origin, roughly 340 B to 166 KB responses derived from page data) gives HTTPS 141,884 vs 127,167 req/s tiny (1.12x) and 1.02x small and medium, with nginx ahead on HTTP tiny 187,973 vs 161,101.
status_note: Archived 2025-08-29 by CloudWeGo as no longer recommended (insufficient engineering resources) despite earlier ByteDance production use; MIT or Apache-2.0, so it can be forked, but it needs Rust nightly, an io_uring kernel and a TLS dependency refresh before production use.
